# Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection

"Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection" is the official title of a haute couture fashion collection designed by the British fashion house Alexander McQueen for the Spring/Summer 2009 season , , . Presented in Paris on October 3, 2008, at a venue that was formerly a morgue, the collection is a significant cultural artifact recognized for its profound thematic depth and theatrical presentation , . It explores the tension between organic forms and industrial aesthetics, interrogating humanity's impact on the environment and our relationship with the natural world , . The collection is structured in two distinct sequences, one evoking nature through soft colors, natural fibers, and digital prints of wood grain, while the second sequence confronts synthetic materials, angular crystal motifs, and imagery of human-engineered landscapes like the Eiffel Tower , . This dichotomy serves as a visual essay on evolution, degeneration, and the potential consequences of human greed on planetary survival . The collection's notability is cemented by its inclusion in major retrospective exhibitions at prestigious institutions such as the Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, which have positioned it as a canonical work in the history of contemporary fashion . Its title itself is a deliberate artistic choice, using typographic rupture ("Dis-tinction," "Un-natural") to critique the language of evolutionary biology and question taxonomic violence and racialized categorization . The full experience of the collection was integral to its meaning, featuring a catwalk filled with antique taxidermy, a rotating globe projection, and an invitation with a lenticular image morphing the designer's face into a human skull, all contributing to a visceral exploration of mortality, beauty, and savagery , .

## Collection Overview and Presentation

Alexander McQueen's Spring/Summer 2009 collection, titled 'Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection', was a meticulously crafted event that transcended mere fashion display to become a total sensory experience , . The presentation took place on October 3, 2008, in Paris, at a venue chosen for its powerful symbolic resonance: a former morgue , . This location immediately established a dark, theatrical atmosphere, priming the audience for a confrontation with themes of mortality, decay, and the boundary between life and death, which are recurrent motifs throughout McQueen's body of work . The entire production was designed as a cohesive artistic environment where every element—from the setting to the garments—worked in concert to deliver the collection's complex message . Central to the runway spectacle was a gallery of antique taxidermy, including an elephant, giraffe, tiger, zebra, and polar bear, arranged along the catwalk , . Models were required to walk directly among these preserved animal forms, transforming the act of walking down the runway into a performative statement about animal exploitation, commodification, and the liminal space between the living and the dead . This centerpiece directly connected the collection to McQueen's broader "Victorian Bestiary" exploration, engaging with post-Darwinian anxieties and critiques of speciesism . Further reinforcing the cosmic scale of the collection's concerns, a large-scale rotating metal globe projected images of the sun, moon, and Earth spinning on its axis, creating a backdrop that underscored the global environmental issues being addressed , .

The conceptual framework of the collection was further reinforced before the show even began. The invitation distributed to guests featured a lenticular image created by Gary James McQueen, which slowly transformed a portrait of Lee McQueen himself into a human skull , . This poignant visual metaphor served as a direct and undeniable prelude to the evening's themes, acting as a stark reminder of mortality and the interplay between nature and artifice . The collection itself was explicitly structured in two distinct sequences, each defined by a different aesthetic philosophy and color palette, representing a clear thematic progression from organic origins to industrial transformation , . The first sequence was characterized by soft colors, natural fibers, and digitally printed patterns of wood grains and meadow flowers , . It incorporated delicate details such as silk flowers encased in tulle, evoking Victorian specimen jars, whitework embroidery, and shimmering beetle-wing sequins , . In contrast, the second sequence embraced synthetic materials like Lycra and bonded leather, alongside a more aggressive and futuristic visual language , . This half of the collection employed angular crystal prints, diamond-to-skeleton morphing motifs, and bell-jar-shaped dresses that visually echoed the collection's taxidermy centerpiece , . The palette shifted dramatically to include black, white, vivid pink, and sapphire, accompanied by jet, gold, and silver Swarovski-encrusted bodysuits that transformed simple silhouettes into glittering, almost surgical pieces of art , . This stark division between the two halves allowed McQueen to explore the full spectrum of his thematic concerns, moving from a representation of nature to a critique of unnatural, human-driven selection processes . The collection notes from McQueen affirmed his intent, stating he was "not aiming to preach" but confirmed his underlying concern that "we’re in danger of killing the planet through greed" .

## Thematic Analysis: Nature vs. Industry

At its core, 'Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection' functions as a powerful visual discourse on the fundamental conflict between the organic and the industrial, exploring humanity's fraught relationship with the natural world . The collection’s dual structure provides a clear narrative arc, beginning with an idealized vision of nature and progressing toward a dystopian future shaped by technology and human intervention , . The first sequence of the show immerses the viewer in a world of organic forms and natural materials, yet even here, the influence of the artificial is present. The use of digitally printed wood grains and meadow flowers on natural fibers represents a synthesis of the real and the simulated, suggesting a nature already mediated by technology , . This sequence draws heavily on traditional craftsmanship and botanical motifs, employing techniques like whitework embroidery and incorporating materials such as silk flowers encased in tulle, which evoke the aesthetic of Victorian-era specimen jars and cabinets of curiosities , . The palette of soft colors reinforces this connection to a more innocent or pristine state of nature , . However, the introduction of beetle-wing sequins adds a touch of iridescent, almost unnatural glamour, hinting at the allure of artifice even within this seemingly naturalistic segment , . This careful blending of authentic and artificial elements sets the stage for the collection's central inquiry: what happens when the boundaries between them dissolve?

The second sequence marks a radical departure, plunging the viewer into a world dominated by industrial aesthetics and synthetic materials , . Here, the tension between nature and industry becomes explicit and confrontational. The shift to materials like Lycra and bonded leather signals a move away from the earthbound qualities of the first half toward a more technological, machine-like sensibility , . The graphic prints in this section are particularly revealing; they feature the iconic silhouette of the Eiffel Tower and jagged granite mountains sourced from Dan Holdsworth’s triptych , . These images represent humanity's most significant architectural and geological interventions, reframing nature not as a pristine wilderness but as a landscape actively reshaped by human ambition and industry , . The morphing motifs, described as diamonds transforming into skeletons, suggest a process of decay or degradation accelerated by unnatural forces, a visual metaphor for how industrial progress can corrupt or destroy its organic origins , . The bell-jar-shaped dresses further develop this theme of containment and observation, linking the garments directly back to the taxidermy centerpiece and suggesting that both nature and the animals themselves have become objects to be studied, controlled, and displayed, much like specimens in a museum , .

This exploration of the boundary between the natural and the unnatural extends beyond materiality into the very concept of selection itself. McQueen’s collection interrogates the idea of natural selection, questioning whether human actions are creating a new, "unnatural" form of evolutionary pressure . The dazzling, Swarovski-encrusted bodysuits, described as "dripping in sparkling crystals," exemplify this concept perfectly . They take a simple, functional garment—the bodysuit—and transform it into an elaborate, ornamental piece of art, prioritizing artificial beauty over utility . This can be seen as a commentary on consumer culture and the artificial standards of beauty imposed upon the human body. Scholarly analysis positions McQueen as a "tailor-surgeon attempting unprecedented grafts" between animal, human, and machine, highlighting a reverse-evolutionary narrative where the line between species and technology blurs . The collection critically reconfigures Victorian aesthetics—such as fur, feathers, and whalebone—not just by using them, but by overlaying them with gothic, surgical, and post-industrial motifs that expose the violence and commodification inherent in their use . Ultimately, the collection presents a bleak vision where the very definition of what is "natural" is under threat. By juxtaposing the delicate beauty of silk flowers with the harsh geometry of industrial prints, and by placing models amidst the silent, preserved bodies of animals, McQueen forces a confrontation with the consequences of human dominance. The final message is unambiguous: the unchecked pursuit of progress and consumption risks killing the very planet that sustains us, leading to a world where nature is either extinct or entirely contained, observed, and made artificial .

## Critical Interpretation of the Title

The title of the collection, 'Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection', is not merely a descriptive phrase but a sophisticated and deliberately provocative intellectual construct that invites deep critical engagement , . The strategic use of spacing and hyphens—placing a break after "Natural" and "Dis-", and another after "Un"-—is a crucial stylistic choice that disrupts familiar terminology and forces the reader to pause and reconsider its meaning . This typographic rupture acts as a visual cue for a deeper interrogation of the terms themselves, signaling an intention to challenge rather than simply describe. The phrase directly engages with Charles Darwin's foundational theory of "natural selection," but it does so by introducing a counter-concept: "unnatural selection" . While "natural selection" describes the gradual process by which organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and produce more offspring, McQueen’s "unnatural selection" implies a force of change that is abrupt, artificial, and driven by external, often destructive, human agency . This reinterpretation elevates the collection from a simple exploration of fashion aesthetics to a complex commentary on modern science, ethics, and the socio-political legacies of evolutionary thought.

The critical weight of the title is significantly amplified when viewed through the lens of mid-to-late 20th-century scientific debates surrounding race and biological determinism. During this period, scholars and activists grappling with the legacy of scientific racism began to implicitly invoke the term "unnatural selection" as a tool to dismantle racist ideologies without resorting to discredited biological explanations . For example, population geneticists like Luigi Luca Cavalli-Sforza and Richard Lewontin demonstrated that the vast majority of human genetic variation occurs within so-called "racial" groups, not between them, thereby undermining the genetic basis for racial classification , . In parallel, cognitive scientists argued that differences in measured IQ between populations were attributable not to innate genetics but to "cultural inheritance"—a social phenomenon rather than a biological one . In these contexts, "unnatural selection" became a politically neutralizing substitute for race, describing social outcomes as products of environment and culture rather than biology . McQueen’s title resonates powerfully with this intellectual history. By co-opting and repurposing this terminology, he subverts its original usage. He takes a term developed to critique biological determinism in the domain of race and applies it to the domain of environmentalism, arguing that the current trajectory of human development is a form of "unnatural selection" driven by greed and industrialization , .

This critical interpretation suggests that the collection is a multi-layered critique that operates on several levels simultaneously. On one level, it is a direct warning about climate change and ecological destruction, a plea for humanity to recognize its destructive impact on the planet . On another, more subtle level, it is a deconstruction of the very language used to classify and hierarchize life. The hyphenation in "Dis-tinction" can be read as a critique of "distinction" itself—a term historically used in taxonomy to create rigid categories, a practice that has been weaponized in the service of racism and oppression . By breaking apart the word, McQueen highlights the arbitrary and constructed nature of such distinctions. Similarly, "Un-natural" challenges the romanticized notion of a pristine, untouched "natural" world, suggesting instead that humanity has always been a part of, and a shaper of, nature, albeit in increasingly destructive ways. The collection thus interrogates the tension between natural and unnatural selection, positing that the greatest threat to the planet may not come from some external, alien force, but from the internal logic of our own civilization, a logic that values artificial growth over sustainable balance . In doing so, McQueen aligns his artistic practice with a long tradition of challenging dominant narratives, using the runway as a platform for critical discourse on some of the most pressing ethical and scientific questions of our time.

## Legacy and Institutional Recognition

The legacy of Alexander McQueen's 'Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection' is firmly established through its enduring presence in academic discourse and its prominent inclusion in major museum exhibitions, which have solidified its status as a canonical work in the canon of contemporary fashion , , . The collection's themes of mortality, environmental crisis, and the grotesque beauty of the natural world found a perfect home in the V&A's influential exhibition *Savage Beauty*, which debuted at the Met in New York in 2011 and later traveled to London . This exhibition curated a narrative around McQueen’s work that emphasized his ability to redefine beauty through marginal, unconventional, and "grotesque" elements, positioning garments from 'Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection' as key examples of this philosophy . The inclusion of a 'Bell Jar' dress from the collection, described as "dripping in sparkling Swarovski crystals," exemplifies this approach, showcasing how McQueen could transform a simple silhouette into a breathtaking, almost surreal piece of art that challenged conventional notions of adornment and elegance . The exhibition's success and subsequent scholarly attention validated the collection's artistic and conceptual importance, ensuring its continued relevance for new generations of viewers and students of fashion.

Following the success of *Savage Beauty*, garments from the Spring/Summer 2009 collection have been featured in numerous other high-profile institutional exhibitions, demonstrating a sustained scholarly interest in its themes and aesthetics. The Columbia Museum of Art hosted the exhibition *Lee Alexander McQueen & Ann Ray: Rendez-Vous* from October 7, 2023, to January 21, 2024, which showcased over 60 photographs by Ann Ray documenting McQueen’s creative process alongside more than 50 garments from his archive , . This exhibition included a 'crystal kaleidoscopic print blazer' and a 'multicolor silk moth print kaleidoscope dress' from 'Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection', contextualizing them within the intimate collaboration between McQueen and Ray , . The New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA) also integrated a piece from the collection into its inaugural major fashion exhibition, *A Queen Within: Adorned Archetypes*. NOMA curated the collection around seven Jungian feminine archetypes, featuring a two-piece ensemble from 'Natural Dis-tinction, Un-natural Selection' as part of its exploration of the "Mother Earth" archetype, using fashion as a medium to tell complex psychological and mythological stories . These exhibitions, organized by Barrett Barrera Projects—the owner of the largest private collection of McQueen's work—ensure that the collection continues to be disseminated and interpreted across multiple cities and academic settings , .

Further cementing the collection's legacy, garments from it have been included in touring exhibitions such as the one at the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM), which ran from October 5, 2024, through January 12, 2025 . The Chertsey Museum has also documented a silk satin suit from the collection, noting its kaleidoscopic digital print of tree bark as a key example of McQueen's exploration of man’s impact on the environment . This extensive institutional validation, spanning retrospectives, thematic exhibitions, and specialized showcases, confirms that 'Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection' is far more than a single moment in fashion history. It is a rich and complex cultural text that continues to be analyzed and celebrated for its profound thematic content, innovative design, and masterful integration of performance and concept. The collection's journey from a runway show held in a former morgue to a series of carefully curated artifacts in world-class museums underscores its enduring power to provoke thought and inspire dialogue about our relationship with nature, technology, and mortality.

50 Years of Fashion
-------------------

It is fifty years since Chertsey Museum first opened its doors in 1965. In order to celebrate this important anniversary, we are delighted to present a display of fashionable women’s wear dating from the 1960s to the present day. The pieces shown in this gallery are selected from the nationally significant Olive Matthews collection of dress, which is held here at Chertsey Museum.

The past fifty years has been a period of unprecedented cultural and technological change. Breakthroughs in space exploration, global communication and travel have all taken place, as well as scientific discoveries, not least relating to the manufacture of new synthetic materials. At the same time, living standards have improved for the majority of people in the western world, and greater freedoms have led to enhanced social equality for many. Fashion has kept pace with society; morphing and mutating in new and often unpredictable ways. The very nature of fashion itself has changed. The mini skirt of the 1960s was perhaps the last ‘universal’ fashion, and the subsequent rise of individualism has fundamentally altered the way that fashion works within society. Now personal choice reigns as a plethora of different styles emerge concurrently and increasingly swiftly, allowing us to select looks according to our own personal circumstances and those of our peer groups.

In the whirl of beautiful and eye-catching styles displayed here a number of themes can be traced. The exhibition is set out chronologically which helps us to understand how fashion progressed. However, when we look back it is easy to fall into the trap of remembering the styles of the past fifty years in terms of the fashions that characterised each decade. When closely considering the looks which emerged over the period, it is clear that they do not fall into such neat categories. The styles of the early 1960s were far more in keeping with those of the late 1950s and the same can be said of each successive period; established and, with hindsight, ‘typical’ fashions only emerged during the middle years of any given decade.

Though it is fun to look back at the trends which were adopted during each successive era, a number of other fascinating themes can also be traced. The growing importance of the younger generation within society as a whole is clearly in evidence. This can be seen in the styles from the mid 1960s onwards which celebrate a youthful body above all things - a quality which has been afforded enormous value by the fashion industry ever since. It is also possible to chart the emancipation of women as they emerged from their tight-waisted and often cumbersome early ‘60s clothes into garments which allowed for more practical participation within society. As well as the adoption of clothing which allowed greater freedom of movement, a conscious shift into the ‘male’ sphere of office work is particularly evident in the ‘power dressing’ of the 1980s. No less fascinating are the more subtle developments that can be linked to fashion trends. For example, the economic downturns of the 1970s and late ‘80s to early ‘90s periods are characterised by nostalgia with historically-inspired clothing as the fashion world sought to retreat into the romance and relative safety of the past. By contrast, economic upturns saw designers pushing boundaries; experimenting with new and forward-thinking concepts as well as indulging in lavish materials. Other social developments such as the greater affordability of overseas travel are also reflected in garments which incorporate exotic and far-flung influences.

In addition to charting different visual links between particular garments, it is hoped that this exhibition will allow visitors to immerse themselves in the fashions of the past fifty years through a range of alternative methods of interpretation. Our dressing up area features replicas and garments inspired by those on display, whilst fashion-related film clips will inform and jog memories. Evocative perfumes from each era are also captured in the coloured scarves found in the reading area. Everyone who views this exhibition will come to it with their own set of recollections and experiences of fashionable styles. We hope that you will take time to reflect on the similarities and differences between these garments and your own personal preferences through the years. A comment book in which you can write down your reactions to the display, including any memories it may have sparked, is located nearby.

### Glancing over one’s shoulder

[![Image 1](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/dress2.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/dress2.jpg&preset=full)

The 1960s was an incredibly important and exciting decade for fashion. It was an era of strong, youth-driven style trends which have remained in the collective consciousness as iconic looks ever since. However, to focus only on garments such as the mini skirt would be to ignore the way most people dressed during the early years of the decade. Apart from a pioneering few, the majority of the population dressed in a way that owed much more to the style of the 1950s.

Fashions which celebrated the overtly feminine, mature figure still held sway. The Post-war designs of a handful of couturiers continued to dominate fashion throughout the 1950s and well into the early ‘60s. These included Christian Dior, who initiated the ‘New Look’ of 1947 (his legacy continued after his untimely death in 1957), and Cristobal Balenciaga, a master at blending cut, construction, fabric and colour. Their tightly boned bodices and wide flowing skirts captured women’s imaginations after the privations of war, and their influence prevailed for many years. Though teenage styles were emerging, for formal occasions young women were still expected to aspire to the style of their mothers. This included the wearing of hats and gloves when in public.

There are several garments displayed in this case which epitomise the look of the early 1960s. Change was afoot with subtle innovations, as seen in the more columnar line of the Hardy Amies gown of eau de nil silk, or the shorter skirts of the boldly printed day dresses, but at this stage no-one could have predicted the radical developments ahead. The apricot brocade ball gown of 1961, with its wide, flowing skirts and tight bodice, was worn by a very young woman. It shows how evening wear, though simplified, remained lavish and romantic. And, just as in the 1950s, many women would still have reached for strong foundation garments, such as the pink corset seen nearby, to help them achieve this soon-to-be-outmoded silhouette.

### The ‘60s in full swing

[![Image 2](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Courr__ges_dress.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Courr__ges_dress.jpg&preset=full)

By the mid-1960s a new and distinct fashionable style had developed. It celebrated a youthful, almost childlike body with bold colours, modern fabrics, sharp, simple lines and often very short skirts.

The fashion revolution which gained momentum after the first few years of the 1960s is defined by a switch from the influence of the older generation to a youthful one. The phenomenon was dubbed ‘Youthquake’ by American Vogue in 1965. A number of subcultures, such as the Teddy Boys and the Mods, had emerged during the ‘50s and early ‘60s. Alongside music, clothing was a hugely important factor in how these groups defined themselves, and aspects of their looks filtered into mainstream youth consciousness. In addition, children who had been born in the ‘Baby Boom’ just after the Second World War were now old enough to earn in a newly buoyant economy. They often spent disposable income on clothing.

Designers able to cater to the needs of a younger generation who yearned for change were also emerging at this time. Often the products of forward-thinking fashion and textile departments in art schools; innovators such as Mary Quant, Foale and Tuffin and John Bates began to design for their own peers. Their garments were sold in small boutiques, many located on London’s King’s Road or Carnaby Street. Soon larger department stores were stocking and copying these new designs. Youthful fashions made by young trendsetters, who in turn were influenced by London street style, were coming to the fore.

On the broader fashion stage, a new group of high-end designers was also blazing a trail. The work of André Courrèges, Pierre Cardin and Paco Rabanne was futuristic in style. They developed memorable and ground-breaking designs, some of which shook the very foundations of the fashion establishment. But the remarkable styles of the 1960s originated not from the rarefied ateliers of the couturier, but from the kids on the street.

### Flower Power to Power Dressing

[![Image 3](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.2010.02a_b_front_1.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.2010.02a_b_front_1.jpg&preset=full)

During the late 1960s fashion altered radically once more with the emergence of the Hippie movement which originated in America, and quickly spread to Britain. Hippies sought to reject set fashion trends which they saw as corporate and dictated from above. Instead they favoured unisex styles and drew inspiration from nature and the garments of ethnic cultures. Individuality was the key. The ‘flower power’ sentiment also led to a great interest in vintage clothing, spawning a preference for soft, romantic, flowing skirts. Despite their best efforts, however, the Hippie movement had simply generated another fashion trend which manufacturers and designers were quick to pick up on.

As the Hippie era faded, their legacy of individualism remained. Fashion became optional, and a range of youth and music led trends emerged. These included the outrageously high platform shoes and bright colour combinations of Glam Rock. By the mid ‘70s Punks were manipulating sexual and political taboos in shocking and radical statements of anarchic display. The late 1970s Disco craze was influential in sexualising fashion with skin tight clothing in shiny fabrics for nightclub wear. In more everyday clothing the second half of the decade saw a new sober mood with skirts slightly below the knee and a much more general adoption of trousers for women - a reflection of the strength of the Women’s Rights Movement.

The scene was set for the excesses of the 1980s. For day, wide-shouldered, masculine ‘Power Suits’ with angular lines dominated, whilst eveningwear celebrated all things opulent and extravagant. The cult of the ‘designer label’ took hold as fashion houses such as Armani and Lacroix were marketed as worldwide brands. The work of Japanese designers such as Rei Kawakubo for Comme Des Garçons, Kansai Yamamoto and Issey Miyake also came to the fore. Dual elements of traditional Japanese dress and radically deconstructed cut offered refreshingly unconventional alternatives to mainstream fashion and continued to find success well into the next decade.

### Global crashes and worldwide trends

The stock market crash of 1987 brought the world back down to earth with a bump. It marked the end of extravagance and by the early 1990s the fashion industry was suffering a crisis of confidence and struggling to react to the new somber mood. Black was the dominant colour during the late 1980s, only to be succeeded by grey in the ‘90s. Grunge, a look that originated with the youth culture of Seattle, was embraced by designers like Anna Sui and Marc Jacobs. Loose, layered clothing such as checked shirts, long dresses and oversized jumpers were worn with heavy Dr. Martin boots. Grunge did not sit easily with the world of high fashion, and consumers were not happy to pay high prices for it. The fashion industry soon returned to more feminine, fitted clothes.

The mid 1990s saw designers like John Galliano and Vivienne Westwood plundering the archives and creating striking collections inspired by historical costume. Westwood designed beautifully cut and characteristically humorous garments, mainly inspired by the 18th century. Alexander McQueen launched his first commercial collection in 1993. Often shocking and dramatic in their presentation, his collections were the result of clear vision and sound design. He was appointed creative director of the House of Givenchy in 1997 and also designed under his own label. His work continued to challenge and excite the fashion world until his death in 2010. The work of other British designers such as Stella McCartney and Matthew Williamson has also been extremely influential. The 21st Century has seen style trends move increasingly swiftly. The availability of fashion for all, with incredibly cheap garments from retailers such as Primark and New Look, has characterized the era. Growth in the worldwide luxury goods market has helped to bolster established fashion houses through the recession which began in 2008. The internet now disseminates fashion brands to a massive worldwide audience, and the cult of celebrity has seen a number of spin-off labels such as Victoria Beckham’s ‘The Collection’. In addition, vintage and vintage-inspired clothes have captured our imagination as never before.

### Multi-coloured day dress, c.1958 - 1960

[![Image 4](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/day_dress_1.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/day_dress_1.jpg&preset=full)

The fitted waist and colourful fabric of this sleeveless day dress are typical of summer dresses of the late ‘50s to early ‘60s. Full skirts were common, but this one differs in cut. Known as a ‘Bubble Skirt’, it puffs out and is then gathered into a band at knee level. The bodice is lined with green rayon and the skirt is supported and stiffened with Vilene interfacing.

### Ball gown from D.H. Evans, 1960 - 1961

[![Image 5](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/DH_Evans.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/DH_Evans.jpg&preset=full)

This ankle-length ball gown is of apricot and white Rayon brocade. A naturalistic pattern of roses is woven into the fabric. The softly pleated bodice is lined with white cotton and the generously cut skirt is unlined. The wide skirts are supported with a replica net petticoat as the original is no longer present. This gown was purchased at D.H. Evans department store, Oxford Street. Founded in 1879, D.H. Evans was eventually taken over in 1954 by department store group House of Fraser and continued to trade under the D.H. Evans name until 1987 when it was re-named House of Fraser. The original store on Oxford Street is now the House of Fraser flagship store. This ball gown was worn to a May Ball in 1961 at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. The original owner remembered wearing it in a punt on the river Cam.

### Evening gown by Hardy Amies, c.1964

[![Image 6](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/dress2.jpg&preset=small)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/dress2.jpg&preset=full)

Made from eau de nil shantung silk, this dress is cut with a shallow round neckline at the front and a ‘V’ shape at the back.  The bodice is beaded in an undulating pattern with diamanté and clear glass beads. Plastic sequins are stitched to make three-dimensional flower shapes. Plainer panels of silk curve around the sides and meet at the centre front with a bow. The long, softly gathered skirt  incorporates a stiffened white rayon underskirt mounted onto white silk organza. The label reads ‘Hardy Amies, 14 Savile Row, W1’. Hardy Amies (1909 - 2003) is known for the pieces he created for Queen Elizabeth II’s wardrobe, for whom he designed between 1952 and 1989. He began his career at the houses of Lachasse and Worth before opening his own business at 14 Savile Row in West London in 1946.

### Suit by Louis Féraud, 1965 - 1968

[![Image 7](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Feraud.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Feraud.jpg&preset=full)

Sold by Harrods, this pink polyester suit comprises a dress and jacket. The dress is sleeveless with a fitted bodice and A-line skirt. It features decorative buttons of pink plastic with gilt metal centres. The short, fitted jacket is simply cut with minimal detailing. The style of the suit is similar to that favoured by Jacqueline Kennedy whose immaculate dress sense was much admired. Louis Féraud (1921-1999) presented his first Haute Couture collections in 1958. During the early ‘60s he hired a number of other talented designers, including Jean Louis Scherrer, and later produced ready-to-wear collections which were sold through high-end retailers. The company is now owned by the German group Escada. There is a shop in Paris and the Féraud label continues to be sold through Harrods.

### Black and white spotted day dress, 1960

[![Image 8](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/spotty.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/spotty.jpg&preset=full)

This summer dress is made from nylon chiffon printed with a bold black spot pattern. The acetate lining has also been printed with black spots which overlap with those on the chiffon creating an interesting blurred effect. The wide skirt and black nylon crêpe of the waistband serve to draw the eye to the centre and accentuate the narrow waist - a look which owed much to the ‘New Look’ of the late 1940s to ‘50s.

### Blue hat, 1960 - 1965

[![Image 9](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/dahlia.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/dahlia.jpg&preset=full)

### Maroon felt hat, 1960 - 1963

[![Image 10](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/fez.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/fez.jpg&preset=full)

They remained in place indoors and out, but the fashion for ‘beehive’ hairstyles led to hats being phased out for everyday wear, never to return in such a general way again.

### Mini dress by André Courrèges, 1967 - 1969

[![Image 11](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Courr__ges_dress.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Courr__ges_dress.jpg&preset=full)

Shown with a modern ribbed sweater, the matt black wool jersey of this striking mini dress contrasts well with its leatherette trim. André Courrèges (b.1923) brought a ground breaking new ‘60s look to Parisian couture. He began his career at the fashion house of

Balenciaga and then started his own label in 1961. In 1964 he stunned the fashion world with a totally modern collection. He was known for the ‘A’ line shape of his mini dresses and also for immaculately cut trouser suits. He was inspired by sportswear and the ultra-modernity of space exploration.

[![Image 12](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/bag.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/bag.jpg&preset=full)

### Corset by Preslei, c.1961 - 1965

[![Image 13](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/corset.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/corset.jpg&preset=full)

### Evening shoes by Clarks, 1956 - 1964

[![Image 14](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/silver_shoe.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/silver_shoe.jpg&preset=full)

Shoes with much longer pointed toes, known as ‘Winklepickers’, were favoured by younger followers of fashion at this time.

[![Image 15](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/gloves.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/gloves.jpg&preset=full)

A pair of ladies white nylon gloves with a diagonal row of three leatherette diamonds along the hand back. ### Evening shoes, Harrods, c.1967

[![Image 16](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/gold_shoe.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/gold_shoe.jpg&preset=full)

Covered with gold lamé fabric, these court shoes have wide, low heels. The glittering gold effect would have lent both opulence and a futuristic feel to an outfit. Their relative simplicity in design is in keeping with the uncluttered lines of mid 1960s fashions. These shoes were originally worn with a full-length evening gown to a 21st birthday party in December 1967.

### Underwear set by Mary Quant, 1967 - 1973

[![Image 17](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/quant.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/quant.jpg&preset=full)

A sheer nylon bra and knickers set in turquoise blue with tiny spots. Mary Quant (b.1934) was one of the originators of the pared down and youth-orientated styles which dominated fashion during the 1960s. She opened her first boutique: Bazaar on King’s Road, London in 1955 and her business went from strength to strength through the 1960s and ‘70s. Quant is often credited with inventing the mini skirt (she herself stated

that the girls on the street invented it first). Shorter skirts led to both brevity and youthfulness in underwear fashions as girdles and suspender belts would have been visible. Tights were now worn and underwear grew smaller and smaller as the youthful physique, which required little extra support, became the ideal. Mary Quant designed underwear which went with her clothes. They often had humorous names such as the ‘Booby Trap’ bra or ‘Highly Strung’ bra and briefs.

### Gown by Ossie Clark for Quorum, c.1974

[![Image 18](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/chert_8.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/chert_8.jpg&preset=full)

This diaphanous full-length silk chiffon gown, with slightly padded silk satin epaulettes and plunging neckline, features Celia Birtwell’s ‘Marie Antoinette’ print design. The cut is reminiscent of 1940s Hollywood glamour. Ossie Clark (1942 - 1996) first found success when his pieces were stocked by Alice Pollock’s Quorum boutique in London’s King’s Road. He later went on to produce a diffusion line for Radley. During his 1965 - 1974 heyday Clark’s incredibly flattering, beautifully cut clothes were worn by many London socialites, making them highly desirable and fashionable. Alongside Bill Gibb, his work popularised the flowing, vintage-style fashions of the late ‘60s and early ‘70s. Ossie was inspired by garments from the V&A’s collections and worked closely with his then wife, the textile designer Celia Birtwell, whose colourful and imaginative prints featured in many of his designs.

[![Image 19](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.1992.1.IMAGE.front.JPG&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.1992.1.IMAGE.front.JPG&preset=full)

### Evening gown by Jean Varon, 1971 - 1974

[![Image 20](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/varon.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/varon.jpg&preset=full)

John Bates (b.1938), launched the label Jean Varon in 1960. He was known for his futuristic work during the mid ‘60s, but pieces became more soft and feminine during the later ‘60s and early ‘70s. [![Image 21](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/skirt.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/skirt.jpg&preset=full)

### Gown by Annie Gough, 1970 - 1974

[![Image 22](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/gough.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/gough.jpg&preset=full)

This full-length evening dress of fine wool has a bold print which is slightly reminiscent of Indian textile designs - a sign that mainstream fashion was drawing inspiration from ethnic hippie-style dress. Green quilted velvet has been added to give weight and structure. Scottish designer Annie Gough began designing clothing in 1967. She wanted to produce ‘elegant, flattering and feminine’ clothes. Her work utilised natural fabrics and retailed for high prices in exclusive boutiques.

### Knitwear ensemble, Bill Gibb, c.1982

[![Image 23](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Gibb.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Gibb.jpg&preset=full)

This three-piece ensemble features geometric patterns in soft heather mauves and browns. Made from acrylic, it is typical of the complex knitwear produced by Gibb and his long-term collaborator Kaffe Fassett. Bill Gibb (1943 - 1988), was a Scottish-born designer who has long been held in high esteem by the fashion cognoscenti. Between 1969 and 1985 he produced a number of ground-breaking and influential collections. Gibb was adept at combining different prints, fabrics, colours and textures and creating a coherent whole. He worked with American -born artist Kaffe Fassett to produce beautiful knitwear pieces. This ensemble dates from the early 1980s when Gibb and Fassett worked with the Leicestershire firm Annette Carol to produce ready-to-wear items in acrylic using a jacquard weave technique.

### Gown by Jean-Louis Scherrer, c.1985

[![Image 24](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Scherrer.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Scherrer.jpg&preset=full)

It is made from pink and green shot silk taffeta with a shirred and ruched bodice. The enormous sleeves are constructed from stiff net and decorated with petals of pink and green silk organza. The large bow at the back extends to form a short train. Jean-Louis Scherrer (1935 - 2013) began his fashion career working for Christian Dior. He then continued under Dior’s successor, Yves Saint Laurent, before being employed by Louis Féraud. He launched his own label in 1962, numbering several celebrities amongst his clients. During the 1980s his work was known for its opulence and luxury. His extremely expensive couture designs were popular with a wealthy Middle Eastern clientele. Sadly the first Gulf War led to a decrease in this market. Scherrer was forced to relinquish control of his company and, in 1992, was controversially fired from his own label.

### Boots by Chelsea Cobbler, c.1970 - 1975

[![Image 25](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Cobbler.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Cobbler.jpg&preset=full)

Made from brown leather, they feature a simple top-stitched double triangle motif. Chelsea Cobbler opened in Draycott Avenue, Chelsea in 1967. They produced high-quality hand-finished boots and shoes and continued to find success throughout the 1970s, opening branches elsewhere in London. Their footwear was also stocked by department stores such as Harrods. The early 1970s saw a fashion for boots of this style, which were worn with knee-length and maxi skirts.

### Platform mules by Sacha, c.1974 - 1975

[![Image 26](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/platform.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/platform.jpg&preset=full)

They are made from leather which has been stamped with a floral design. Though some could be as high as 6 or 7 inches, these are a mere 5 inches off the ground. Platform soles were a mainstream fashion of the mid 1970s. They were popularised by glam rock stars such as David Bowie and Elton John.

### Suede Boots by Bruno Magli, 1975 - 1980

[![Image 27](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/boot_shoe.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/boot_shoe.jpg&preset=full)

With their narrow, pointed heels, angled tops and toes tapering to a rounded point, these ankle boots mark the end of the era of the platform. They herald the start of a more sophisticated aesthetic in fashion which took hold during the second half of the 1970s and into the early ‘80s. Bruno Magli is a high-end Italian shoe brand which continues to trade today.

### Court shoes by Miss Holmes, c.1984

[![Image 28](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/woven_shoe.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/woven_shoe.jpg&preset=full)

They have woven navy and white check leather front quarters and a low stiletto heel. The shape, similar to that of the early 1960s, represents a return to lighter, more feminine shoes after the heavier styles favoured during the 1970s. ‘Miss Holmes’ was a brand marketed by Edwards and Holmes, shoe manufacturer of Norwich - a town with a rich history of shoe production. The company was taken over by Van Dal Shoes in 1987 after financial difficulties.

### Suit by Thierry Mugler, 1985 - 1987

[![Image 29](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.2010.02a_b_front_1.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.2010.02a_b_front_1.jpg&preset=full)

An example of a mid-1980s ‘Power Suit’, it consists of a wool and polyester mix jacket and black wool skirt. The oversized jacket has wide, padded shoulders and a narrow waist. Top stitching and welt seams draw attention to its armour-like structure and the sleeves are cut in the raglan style. The simple nature of the pencil-skirt serves to further emphasise the boldness of the jacket. Thierry Mugler (b.1948), is known for his highly structured clothes. He opened his first boutique in Paris in 1978 and found great success during the 1980s and ‘90s. He was one of the first designers to explore the idea of ‘Power Dressing’. Suits such as this one were associated with career women who were entering the male-dominated world of business. The style played with the ideas of power, androgyny and sexuality in an era of conspicuous consumption.

### Dress by Yohji Yamamoto, c.1983 - 1986

[![Image 30](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Yamamoto.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Yamamoto.jpg&preset=full)

It is made from black voile (a very fine wool fabric sometimes known as ‘nun’s veiling’) and silk damask woven with an oriental-style pattern. The sleeves are loosely held together with faggotting stitches in grey thread. The oversized and draped style of this dress is typical of Yamamoto’s work. Yohji Yamamoto

(b.1943), is known for his exceptional skill as a cutter. He established his own studio in Tokyo in 1972, but made his name in Paris in the 1980s alongside other Japanese designers such as Issey Miyake and Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons. His layered, loosely cut garments are designed to swathe the body and often feature asymmetrical lines. He is known for working in black, and experiments with unusual textile forms; often combining different materials as seen in this piece.

### Dress by Issey Miyake, 2009

[![Image 31](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.2010.26_front.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.2010.26_front.jpg&preset=full)

This effortlessly classic ‘Pleats Please’ dress is made from polyester. It has been cut and stitched in a size three times larger than the finished piece before being passed through a heated press in order to produce permanent pleats. Issey Miyake (b.1938), launched his famous ‘Pleats Please’ range in 1993. Echoing Classical Greek garments and the ‘Delphos’ gowns of Mariano Fortuny, the style sheathes the body in neatly structured, yet fluidly organic lines.

### Shoes by Red or Dead, 1996 - 1997

[![Image 32](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/red_or_dead.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/red_or_dead.jpg&preset=full)

They are of gun metal grey coated leather and have high ‘Louis’ style heels. The Red or Dead label was started in 1982 by Wayne Hemmingway (b.1961). The firm became a familiar name on high streets during the 1990s, and was known for producing garments that were both highly fashionable and quirky.

### Sweater by John Smedley, c.1998

[![Image 33](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Smedley.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Smedley.jpg&preset=full)

Of yellow merino wool, it is printed with bull dogs and features a small plastic Wedgwood style cameo which has been stitched to the centre front. A further small bulldog print is found at the back of the neck. This piece was designed by Scott Henshall (b.1975) for the John Smedley knitwear firm (established 1784) and was sold at Liberty’s department store, London.

### Corset by Vivienne Westwood, 1991

[![Image 34](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.2000.25.front.JPG&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/M.2000.25.front.JPG&preset=full)

Designed as part of the 1991 ‘Dressing Up’ collection, this corset is made from stretchy imitation leather.

Vivienne Westwood (b.1941) found fame designing punk fashions with Malcolm McLaren in the 1970s. by the mid 1980s her own label was well established. Her beautifully tailored, often humorous pieces are frequently inspired by historic dress. This 18th century style corset shape appeared in her 1987 ‘Harris Tweed’ collection and she returned to it throughout the 1990s.

### Shoes by Emma Hope, 2003

[![Image 35](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Emma_Hope.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/Emma_Hope.jpg&preset=full)

They are of pink velvet with metal tape and beaded decoration. The sling-back style, low ‘Louis’ heel and long, pointed toes are typical of shoe fashions of the early 2000s.

Shoe designer Emma Hope (b.1967) studied at Cordwainer’s College, East London. She worked for Betty Jackson and Jean Muir before opening her own shops selling exquisitely decorative and delicately feminine shoes.

### Gown by Alexander McQueen, 2007

[![Image 36](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/mcqueen_dress.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/mcqueen_dress.jpg&preset=full)

This darkly striking evening gown is reminiscent of more extreme versions of similar styles found in McQueen’s 2001 Voss and 2005 It’s Only a Game collections. The back is cut daringly low and sharp godets extend from the bugle-beaded bodice; contrasting with the softly layered ballet-style silk tulle skirt.

### Suit by Alexander McQueen, 2009

[![Image 37](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/mcquuen_suit.jpg&preset=)](https://chertseymuseum.org/public_scripts/resizer.php?file=../domains/chertseymuseum.org/local/media/images/medium/mcquuen_suit.jpg&preset=full)

Made from silk satin, this suit was part of McQueen’s 2009 Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection collection. The structured jacket and pleated short skirt feature a kaleidoscopic digital print of tree bark. The juxtaposition of natural materials and digital imagery fit with the theme of the collection which explored the concept of man’s impact on the environment. McQueen (1969 - 2010) also used digital prints extensively in his 2010 Plato’s Atlantis show and they are frequently imitated in high-street fashion.

Images by John Chase Photography

Spring/Summer 2009; Le 104, 5 Rue Curial, Paris; 3 October 2008

McQueen’s Spring/Summer 2009 collection was presented on a catwalk filled with antique taxidermy – including an elephant, giraffe, tiger, zebra and polar bear – in an art space that was formerly a Paris morgue. It was a fitting venue for a collection that was to interrogate the impact of humanity on the environment. Mounted on a plinth at the back of the sloping concrete catwalk stood a metal globe onto which images of a glowing sun, silver moon and the earth rotating on its axis were projected. The show invitation featured a lenticular by Gary James McQueen, the designer’s nephew, in which the image of McQueen’s face morphed into a human skull, hinting at the vulnerability of life.

The primary inspirations behind the collection coalesced around Charles Darwin, the Industrial Revolution and, in particular, the impact of the destructive nature of man. McQueen divided the collection into two sequences to convey his message. The first featured organic shapes, soft colours and natural fibres digitally printed with images of the earth’s natural materials – wood grains and meadow flowers – that were engineered for each garment. These designs placed the natural and the technological in provocative juxtaposition. While dresses cut from a single piece of fabric connoted historical simplicity, silk flowers trapped in tulle referenced Victorian specimen jars. Although decorative touches were predominantly soft – whitework embroidery and beetle-wing sequins – metallic buttercups on mini dresses dripped with acid-yellow enamels and provided a point of contrast.

The second sequence continued to draw inspiration from natural forms – flowers, crystals and minerals – but here they were engineered with a hard edge and enhanced to convey the synthetic qualities associated with modernity and the human touch. Prints were angular and invoked crushed crystal, metallic structures such as the Eiffel Tower and a granite mountain that was borrowed from a Dan Holdsworth triptych. In one design a diamond print morphed into a human skeleton. Dresses shaped like bell-jars and bodysuits encrusted with jet, gold and silver Swarovski crystals conveyed harsh lines in material form. Sharper silhouettes were complemented by a colour palette that incorporated  
black and white as well as vivid pinks and sapphires, and synthetic materials that included Lycra and bonded leather.

Whilst McQueen stated in the collection notes that he was ‘not aiming to preach’, his belief that ‘we’re in danger of killing the planet through greed’ was fundamental.
